title.source: Checking a claim before you share it

essentialQuestion.source: How can you find out if a story is true before you share it?

read.sections.0.heading.source: Ask three questions before you share

read.sections.0.text.source: Messages can spread very quickly, and a shocking story often travels fastest. In Brightwater, a page called Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town bridge would close for a whole year. It said, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like these push people to hurry, and hurrying makes it easy to share something false. Before you share, ask three questions. Who is behind the information? What is the evidence? What do other sources say? The Brightwater post gives no names, no evidence and no link to the town council, which looks after the bridge.
read.sections.0.text.back: Messages can spread very fast, and a shocking story often spreads fastest. In Brightwater, a page called Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town bridge would be closed for a whole year. The page wrote, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like this push people to hurry, and hurrying makes it easy for us to share something false. Before sharing, ask three questions. Who is behind this information? What is its evidence? What do other sources say? That Brightwater post gives no names, no evidence, and no link to the town council, which looks after the bridge.

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people judge real websites about social issues: 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 professional fact-checkers and 25 university students. Most historians and students stayed on one page and read it from top to bottom. Official-looking pages often fooled them. The fact-checkers left the page quickly and opened other sources to find out who was behind it. This is called lateral reading, which means reading sideways across many sources instead of down one page. The fact-checkers reached better answers in much less time.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people judge real websites about social issues: 10 historians who teach at universities, 10 professional fact-checkers and 25 university students. Most historians and students stayed on one page and read it from top to bottom. Pages that looked official often fooled them. The fact-checkers quickly left that page and opened other sources to find out who was behind it. This is called lateral reading, which means reading sideways across many sources, not reading down one page. The fact-checkers got better answers in much less time.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University in the United States watched 45 people check real websites. There were 10 historians who teach at universities. There were 10 fact-checkers and 25 students. Most historians and students read one page, top to bottom. A page that looked official often fooled them. The fact-checkers left the page fast. They opened other sources to find out who made it. This is called lateral reading. It means reading sideways. The fact-checkers got better answers, faster.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 2017, researchers at Stanford University, United States, did a study. They watched 45 people check real websites. There were 10 historians who teach at universities. There were 10 fact-checkers and 25 university students. Most historians and students read one page, from top to bottom. A page that looked official often fooled them. The fact-checkers quickly left that page. They opened other sources to find out who made it. This is called lateral reading. It means reading sideways. The fact-checkers got better answers, faster.

read.sections.2.text.source: Agreement helps only when sources have their own evidence. The town council looks after the bridge, so it knows the dates: two days of repairs, not a whole year. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the council and say the same. A chat page that copies the first post word for word adds no evidence at all. So the first post is false. Don't share it; share the council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, for example with no internet. Then ask a teacher or wait. News can change, so check again later, for example if the repairs take longer.
read.sections.2.text.back: Sameness between sources only helps if each source has its own evidence. The town council looks after the bridge, so the council knows the dates: two days of repairs, not a whole year. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the town council and say the same thing. A chat page that copies the first post word for word adds no evidence at all. So that first post is false. Don't share that post; share the town council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, for example because there is no internet. Then ask a teacher or wait first. News can change, so check again later, for example if the repairs turn out to take longer.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Agreement" (between sources) became "kesamaan antarsumber" (sameness between sources); check it reads naturally.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Do sources agree? That helps only if they have their own evidence. The council looks after the bridge. It says two days. Sometimes you can't check a claim, like with no internet. Ask a teacher, or wait. News can change. So check again later.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Do the sources agree? That only helps if they have their own evidence. The town council looks after the bridge. The council says two days. The radio and the fact-checkers asked the town council. A chat page copied that post. Copying adds no evidence. So the first post is false. Don't share it. Share the town council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, for example without internet. Ask a teacher, or wait. News can change. So check again later.

watch.summary.source: This short video explains lateral reading. It is a way to check information that professional fact-checkers use. Many people check a website by reading down the page. They look at how it looks and what it says about itself. But a page can look serious and still give false or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do something different. After a quick look, they leave the page. They open new pages and search for what other sources say about it and about who is behind it. By reading less of the page and more about it, they learn more, and they learn it faster. You can do the same thing. Before you trust a page, find out who made it and what others say about it.
watch.summary.back: This short video explains lateral reading. It is a way of checking information used by professional fact-checkers. Many people check a website by reading down its page. They look at how it looks and what the page says about itself. But a page can look serious and still give false or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do something different. After a quick look, they leave that page. They open new pages and look for what other sources say about that page and about who is behind it. By reading less of that page and more about it, they know more, and faster. You can do the same thing. Before trusting a page, find out who made it and what other people say about it.

educatorNotes.0.source: This builds on Our World Lesson 23 (What makes information trustworthy?), which teaches source, date and context. This lesson adds lateral reading, and that agreement counts only when sources have their own evidence: the radio and the fact-checkers both asked the council, and the chat page only copied the post. If a class uses both courses, start by recalling Lesson 23's checks.
educatorNotes.0.back: This lesson continues Lesson 23 in the course Exploring Our World (What makes information trustworthy?), which teaches source, date and context. This lesson adds lateral reading, and that sameness between sources only counts if each source has its own evidence: the radio and the fact-checkers both asked the town council, and the chat page only copied the post. If a class uses both courses, start by recalling the ways of checking in Lesson 23.

educatorNotes.1.source: The research in section 2 is Wineburg and McGrew (Stanford History Education Group working paper, 2017; a shortened version in Teachers College Record, 2019). The 45 participants were 10 PhD historians teaching at four-year colleges or universities, 10 professional fact-checkers and 25 first-year Stanford undergraduates. They judged live websites and searched the web on social and political issues, for example comparing two doctors' groups' pages on bullying and finding who was behind a site on the minimum wage. The authors note the small samples and timed tasks. The group became the independent Digital Inquiry Group in January 2024.
educatorNotes.1.back: The research in section 2 is by Wineburg and McGrew (Stanford History Education Group working paper, 2017; its shortened version in Teachers College Record, 2019). The 45 participants were 10 historians with doctorates teaching at four-year colleges or universities, 10 professional fact-checkers and 25 first-year Stanford students. They judged live websites and searched the internet on social and political issues, for example comparing two doctors' associations' pages about bullying and finding who was behind a site about the minimum wage. The authors note the samples were small and the tasks were timed. The group became the independent Digital Inquiry Group in January 2024.

educatorNotes.2.source: Lateral reading normally needs the internet. On an offline device the activity's source cards stand in for new pages; in class, a teacher can play “the other sources” on paper.
